findings.topic: Canonical phase flow as THIS install declares it (bmad-help.csv is the source of truth)
findings.detail:
`bmad-help` reads `_bmad/_config/bmad-help.csv` as its catalog and routes off the `phase`, `preceded-by`, `followed-by`, `required`, `output-location`, `outputs` columns. Its own doc states: numbered phases flow in order; `preceded-by`/`followed-by` are SOFT suggestions; `required=true` is the actual gate; completion is detected by globbing the `outputs` pattern at the resolved `output-location`.

**1-analysis** (all optional): bmad-brainstorming [BP] → brainstorming session; bmad-market-research [MR], bmad-domain-research [DR], bmad-technical-research [TR] → research documents; bmad-product-brief [CB] → product brief; bmad-prfaq [WB] → prfaq document (explicit alternative to the brief).
**2-planning**: bmad-prd [PRD] **required**, preceded-by bmad-product-brief → prd; bmad-ux [CU] optional, preceded-by bmad-prd → ux design.
**3-solutioning**: bmad-architecture [CA] **required** → architecture; bmad-create-epics-and-stories [CE] **required**, preceded-by bmad-architecture → epics and stories; bmad-check-implementation-readiness [IR] **required**, preceded-by bmad-create-epics-and-stories → readiness report.
**4-implementation**: bmad-sprint-planning [SP] **required** → sprint status; then the story cycle — bmad-create-story:create [CS] **required** → bmad-create-story:validate [VS] → bmad-dev-story [DS] **required** → bmad-code-review [CR] → (issues: back to DS; approved: next CS, or ER if epic complete) → bmad-retrospective [ER]. Sidecars: bmad-sprint-status [SS], bmad-checkpoint-preview [CK], bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests [QA] (explicitly "NOT for code review or story validation"), bmad-investigate [IN].
**anytime**: bmad-document-project [DP], bmad-generate-project-context [GPC], bmad-quick-dev [QQ], bmad-correct-course [CC], bmad-agent-tech-writer actions [WD/US/MG/VD/EC], and the whole core band [BSP/PM/BH/ID/SD/EP/ES/AR/ECH/SP(spec)/BC/FI].

findings.topic: How the spec kernel (bmad-spec) relates to bmad-prd / bmad-architecture / bmad-create-epics-and-stories
findings.detail:
bmad-spec is NOT a phase step. It is a **core-module, `anytime` skill** that sits orthogonal to the bmm ceremony chain, and it is described as "the canonical transformer for the BMad spec-kernel ecosystem" whose output is "the machine contract every downstream BMad skill consumes".

Mechanics: it takes ANY intent input (brain dump, PRD, GDD, RFC, brief, transcript, mockups, multi-source) and emits `SPEC.md` carrying a five-field kernel — **Why, Capabilities, Constraints, Non-goals, Success signal** — plus companion files, into `{output_folder}/specs/spec-{slug}/`. Capabilities carry stable `CAP-N` IDs, never reused or renumbered.

The load-bearing design point: `SPEC.md` is **derived**, never hand-edited. `.memlog.md` is the append-only canonical record; `SPEC.md` and spec-authored companions are re-rendered from it on every run. The skill states this explicitly as the reason the ceremony skills compose: *"Deriving the contract from a living log instead of editing the contract in place is what lets the steps around the spec (PRD, UX, architecture, epics) run in any order and feed the same spec without merge drift."* bmad-spec is the **single writer** of SPEC.md; an external hand-edit is unsupported and is overwritten on the next derive.

Relation to each named skill:
- **vs bmad-prd** — substitutes for it upward and downward. bmad-spec explicitly declines to coach: if input is too thin to distill it stops and suggests `bmad-prd`. Conversely bmad-prd's misroute scan at activation redirects to `bmad-quick-dev`/`bmad-product-brief`/`bmad-prfaq`, and a finished PRD is a legitimate bmad-spec *input* — a PRD fully absorbed goes in SPEC.md frontmatter `sources:` (downstream does NOT read it); a PRD still needed downstream goes in `companions:`.
- **vs bmad-architecture** — tightly coupled, bidirectional. "A spec package (`SPEC.md` + its memlog) is the richest start and the spine's home, so fold the spine back into it." bmad-architecture prefers reading a `.memlog.md` over re-reading its source; if input is too thin it suggests `bmad-spec` first; if it must capture missing answers it writes them into a shared spec workspace **through the same `memlog.py`** so bmad-spec can later derive SPEC.md without drift. At close, bmad-architecture's TOP recommendation is to invoke `bmad-spec` to adopt the spine as an **adopted companion** with `AD` IDs kept stable.
- **vs bmad-create-epics-and-stories** — downstream consumer. bmad-architecture's close routes `bmad-spec` → then `bmad-create-epics-and-stories` (or `bmad-create-story` at epic altitude). Companion discovery is the contract: "every consumer reads `companions:` in SPEC.md frontmatter". Note that bmad-create-epics-and-stories' own step-01 discovery globs only look for `*prd*`, `*architecture*` and `ux-designs/ux-*` under planning_artifacts — it has **no** SPEC.md glob, so a spec-first path must be handed to it manually via its "any other documents to include?" prompt.

Companion taxonomy: **spec-authored** (siblings of SPEC.md, bmad-spec owns and edits them — `glossary.md`, `stack.md`, `conventions.md`, `brownfield.md`, `architecture-diagrams.md`, `failure-modes.md`) vs **adopted** (written by an upstream skill, referenced by relative path, never edited — e.g. a UX run's `DESIGN.md`/`EXPERIENCE.md`, or `project-context.md`). Diagrams ALWAYS go in a companion; the kernel holds prose only. Governed by 8 numbered "Spec Law" rules enforced by a two-pass self-validate (Coherence, then Preservation).

findings.topic: Cross-cutting mechanics every skill shares (relevant to planning a real workflow)
findings.detail:
Four conventions recur across the modern skills and should shape any workflow we design:
1. **Customization resolution** — every skill's first activation step is `resolve_customization.py --skill {skill-root} --key workflow`, merging `{skill-root}/customize.toml` → `_bmad/custom/{skill-name}.toml` (team) → `_bmad/custom/{skill-name}.user.toml` (user). Merge rule stated in every customize.toml: *scalars: override wins • arrays: append*. Every `customize.toml` is headed "DO NOT EDIT -- overwritten on every update."
2. **memlog as the run's memory** — bmad-spec, bmad-prd, bmad-architecture and bmad-ux all write `.memlog.md` via `uv run _bmad/scripts/memlog.py {init,append} --workspace <folder> --type <...> --text "..."`, append-only, atomic, never hand-edited. bmad-prd is blunt: "whatever isn't logged is lost on resume."
3. **Resume semantics** — bmad-prd scans `prd_output_path` for run folders whose `prd.md` frontmatter `status` is not `final` and offers resume; bmad-architecture offers resume from an existing run folder's memlog; bmad-spec re-enters the same folder on the same `{slug}` and preserves `CAP-N` IDs. Frontmatter `status: draft|final` + `updated` is the completion signal bmad-help globs for.
4. **Two skill architectures coexist** — the *modern narrative* skills (bmad-spec, bmad-prd, bmad-architecture, bmad-ux) with intent detection, memlog derivation, parallel review subagents and a `finalize_reviewers` gate; and the older *step-file* skills (bmad-create-epics-and-stories, bmad-check-implementation-readiness) with strict just-in-time step loading, `stepsCompleted` frontmatter, and mandatory halt-at-menu behaviour ("NEVER load multiple step files simultaneously", "ALWAYS halt at menus"). The 3-solutioning handoff crosses that boundary, which is where the glob mismatch above bites.

summary: W1 is a working, single-mode macOS menu-bar dictation app (~2,481 LOC Python across `w1_core`/`w1_macos`/`w1_data`) on branch `wip/settings-ui` (HEAD `be59260`, in sync with origin, working tree clean apart from two stray `* 2` duplicate files). The live pipeline is: hotkey → sounddevice capture → Whisper (MLX/faster/mock behind a Protocol) → artifact + confidence gate → deterministic correction (cleanup → mask protected → conservative fuzzy canonical-spelling snap → unmask) → clipboard paste. The single most important thing to know: the `wip/settings-ui` commit **deleted the entire multi-mode correction system** that `main` had. `CorrectionMode` (dictation/document/raw/**gujarati**), the 64 mode-tagged terminology rules, and the Gujarati katha path were all removed from the live code path, but two files were left behind as orphans — `correction/rules.py` is now dead and would raise `AttributeError` if ever called, and `correction/transliterate.py` (127 lines of a complete Gujarati→ā-only-Roman transliterator) is imported by nothing, with its 40-line test file deleted in the same commit. Much of `PLAN.md`, `docs/UI-PLAN.md`, `docs/base44-ui-prompt.md`, `ui/index.html` and the `web/` marketing site still describe the deleted multi-mode world plus never-built features (history, glossary management, meetings/diarization, streaming, onboarding wizard, eval harness). findings.topic: Pipeline — the single core entrypoint (real, working)
findings.detail: `transcribe_and_correct(audio, config, *, backend=None)` is the only core entrypoint. Order: select_backend → build_initial_prompt(bias_token_budget) → backend.transcribe(audio, initial_prompt, language) → strip → artifact gate → confidence gate → correct(). Returns `InjectResult(text, raw, applied, gated, gated_reason)` where gated_reason is "artifact" or "low_confidence". The artifact denylist is a hardcoded 9-item set of Whisper silence-hallucinations ("", ".", "you", "thank you.", "thanks for watching!", "[blank_audio]", …). Confidence gate averages per-segment `no_speech_prob` and `avg_logprob` across segments and never gates when `raw.segments` is empty (mock backend can't be gated).

findings.topic: ASR backends — three, behind a runtime-checkable Protocol
findings.detail: `TranscriptionBackend` Protocol: `transcribe(audio, *, initial_prompt=None, language=None) -> TranscriptionResult(text, language, segments[Segment(start,end,text,avg_logprob,no_speech_prob)])`. `select_backend` dispatches: backend=="mock" → MockBackend; backend=="mlx" or ("auto" and platform.machine()=="arm64") → try `import mlx` presence check then MLXWhisperBackend, re-raising only if mlx was explicitly requested; otherwise falls through to FasterWhisperBackend. Both ML backends lazy-import inside `transcribe()` so importing `w1_core` never pulls the ML stack. FasterWhisper aliases `mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo` → `large-v3-turbo` and caches the model on first transcribe. MockBackend returns canned text with no segments.

findings.topic: Correction engine — what ACTUALLY runs today
findings.detail: `correct(text, config)` is exactly four steps and has NO mode parameter: (1) cleanup_text if config.cleanup.enabled; (2) mask_protected; (3) snap_fuzzy if config.fuzzy.enabled; (4) unmask_protected. There is deliberately no word substitution — the module docstring states "temple" stays "temple", "saint" stays "saint"; only the SPELLING of specialised terms the user actually says is snapped to canonical. `engine.py`'s own package `__init__.py` docstring still describes the removed "ordered mode-enabled regex families" — stale text.

findings.topic: Correction stage — fuzzy.py (the workhorse)
findings.detail: `snap_fuzzy(text, *, min_similarity=0.88, min_term_length=4)` regex-walks `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z’'\-]*` tokens. A token is skipped if: shorter than min_term_length, contains an apostrophe, is ALL-CAPS, is in `data.in_vocab`, or is in the English word set (`/usr/share/dict/words` ∪ a ~90-word bundled `_COMMON_EN` fallback). Otherwise rapidfuzz `process.extractOne(scorer=fuzz.ratio)` against the target keys with `score_cutoff=relaxed` (max(78.0, primary−8)); it snaps if score ≥ primary (88) OR (jellyfish.metaphone key matches AND score ≥ relaxed AND len ≥ 5). Case is matched forward from the original token. Targets are built from `canonical_by_lower` filtered to len ≥ 4, plus a space/hyphen-stripped compact variant.

findings.topic: Correction stage — protect.py, cleanup.py, bias_prompt.py
findings.detail: protect.py masks the 20 protected terms with a U+F8FF-wrapped index sentinel before fuzzy runs, restores in reverse order, and preserves casing so the name "Maya" survives as "Maya". cleanup.py removes standalone fillers (um/uh/er/erm/hmm) and optionally rewrites "X, I mean Y" → Y; self-correction is OFF by default in config. bias_prompt.py packs bias-seed terms into `"Glossary: a, b, c."` under a conservative ~1.3-tokens-per-word estimate, budget default 224.

findings.topic: DEAD CODE — transliterate.py is fully orphaned (exact answer to the transliterate question)
findings.detail: WHAT IT DOES: `transliterate_gujarati(text)` converts **Gujarati script** (Unicode block U+0A80–U+0AFF) to Roman. DIACRITICS EMITTED: exactly one — `ā` (U+0101, the long-a macron), per "House Rules §2.2 (BAPS)"; every other diacritic is stripped, so output is ASCII + ā only. DATA SOURCE: hardcoded Python dicts inside the file — 14 independent vowels, 34 consonants, 13 matras, 10 Gujarati digits — NOT w1_data. Algorithm: syllable walk with an inherent-'a' schwa marker (\x01) resolved at the end; word-final schwa deleted (મંદિર→mandir) but medial schwa kept; anusvara assimilates to m before p/b/m else n; chandrabindu→n, visarga→h, nukta/avagraha/standalone virama dropped; non-Gujarati chars pass through unchanged. STATUS: imported by nothing anywhere in the repo — the only occurrence of the name outside the file is its own `def` line. Its test file `tests/core/test_transliterate.py` (40 lines, 8 parametrised term cases) was DELETED in the current HEAD commit. It is unreachable code, a leftover of the removed `CorrectionMode.gujarati` katha path.

summary: Wispr Flow is a cloud-first AI dictation layer for macOS/Windows/iOS/Android. The core loop is press-and-hold Fn (Mac) to dictate into any focused text field, with text inserted via a clipboard paste + Accessibility API; a hands-free toggle (Fn+Space) exists for long-form. Its differentiation over plain STT is a post-transcription LLM pass: Smart Formatting, Backtrack (filler/false-start removal), per-app-category tone Styles, a synced personal/team Dictionary with auto-learning from your typed corrections, voice-triggered Snippets, Transforms/Polish (rewrite highlighted text via hotkey), and Command Mode (spoken instructions, Pro-gated). It is deeply context-aware: by default it reads the active app's accessibility tree — text before/after/selected around the cursor, on-screen text, conversation history, app identity — and optionally a full-screen screenshot for OCR, and ships that context to Wispr's servers with every dictation request. The Insights surface (desktop-only) has Your Usage / Your Voice / Leaderboard tabs with a WPM radial gauge + percentile, "Corrections by Flow", cumulative total words with MoM delta, a usage-by-app-category bar chart, and a streak heatmap. Notetaker (Mac-only, beta) captures system audio locally with no bot joining, but requires Private Cloud Sync. CRITICALLY FOR w1: essentially every intelligence feature is cloud-dependent. Wispr's own docs state "Transcription always occurs on the cloud" and "Wispr Flow runs entirely in the cloud and is delivered as multi-tenant SaaS"; there is no offline mode on any platform. Only the local history store and Notetaker's audio capture are on-device. This means w1's 100%-on-device stance is architecturally opposed to Wispr's, and parity scope should be defined as "which of these features can be reproduced with local models" rather than "match the feature list".

findings.topic: Core dictation loop — default hotkeys (push-to-talk)
findings.detail: Mac: press and hold Fn (fallback Ctrl+Opt on Macs without an Apple Fn key). Windows: press and hold Ctrl+Win. Docs: "Flow listens while you hold the hotkey" and then "pastes your formatted text into the field." The loop is: click into a text field → hold hotkey → hear a ping / see animated white bars → speak → release → text is inserted. Press ESC to cancel. Hotkey config allows up to 4 shortcuts of up to 3 keys each; single keys alone and common OS shortcuts (Cmd+C/Cmd+V) are blocked, and left/right variants of the same modifier can't be combined. Mouse buttons (middle click, Mouse 4-10) are allowed as modifiers.

findings.topic: Hands-free / toggle mode is a separate binding, not a mode switch
findings.detail: Hands-free is Fn+Space (Mac; Ctrl+Opt+Space fallback) and Ctrl+Win+Space (Windows). Three ways to start it: the hands-free shortcut, clicking the centre of the Flow Bar, or DOUBLE-TAPPING the push-to-talk shortcut (e.g. tapping Fn twice). It ends on shortcut press again, the stop button, or Escape. Behavioural difference worth copying: during hands-free, clicking the Flow Bar does NOT stop recording (it does in push-to-talk). No automatic silence detection is documented — only hard caps. "press enter" works only in hands-free mode.

findings.topic: Text insertion mechanism — clipboard-paste with restore, plus target-field tracking
findings.detail: Flow "tracks which text field you clicked into when you started dictating and inserts your text there in supported apps." On desktop it temporarily hijacks the clipboard to paste, then restores the previous clipboard contents. There is an explicit fallback path: if auto-insert fails, a notification prompts manual paste via a dedicated paste-last-text binding — Cmd+Ctrl+V on Mac, Shift+Alt+Z on Windows. Insertion relies on the macOS Accessibility permission (granted at onboarding so Flow can "insert spoken words into other apps"). Dedicated docs exist for hard targets: IDEs (Cursor/VS Code), remote desktops (RDP/Citrix/VDI), Linux/WSL/terminals, Outlook, and notification reply boxes / browser address bars — i.e. insertion reliability is a known long-tail problem area.

findings.topic: Latency claim — sub-700ms p99 end-to-end, verified at infrastructure source
findings.detail: Baseten (Wispr's inference provider) case study states: "Flow's entire pipeline, from speech recognition models to Llama-based transcript enhancement, runs end-to-end in under 700 milliseconds" — and this is p99, not average. The LLM cleanup stage generates 100+ tokens in under 250ms. Architecture: unnamed ASR models + fine-tuned Llama models for transcript enhancement, served via TensorRT-LLM and Baseten Chains on AWS. This is a useful hard target for w1: a local pipeline must beat ~700ms p99 from key-release to text-inserted to feel equivalent.

findings.topic: Headline speed marketing claim
findings.detail: "4x faster than typing" — framed as ~220 WPM dictation vs ~45 WPM typing. Independent hands-on testing reports 150–180 WPM cleanly handled for conversational English, with punctuation inference strong enough that users rarely need to say "comma" or "period" aloud. Note the 220 WPM figure is a marketing ceiling, not a measured average.

findings.topic: Smart Formatting — the post-ASR formatting pass
findings.detail: Enabled by default on all platforms (only iOS exposes an on/off toggle). Behaviours: (1) cursor-context capitalisation — "Flow lowercases the start of your dictation so it flows with the surrounding text; at the start of a sentence, text stays capitalized", plus automatic leading/trailing space insertion; (2) app-specific trailing-period removal in messaging apps (WhatsApp, Slack, Discord), conditional on the active Writing Style — Formal preserves all periods; (3) spoken list generation from "one… two…" or "first… second…"; (4) explicit spoken punctuation names ("em dash", "ellipsis", "hashtag") with variant recognition; (5) multilingual formatting coverage including Chinese variants, Cantonese, Russian.

findings.topic: Backtrack — in-line self-correction without stopping
findings.detail: Lets you correct mid-sentence while still dictating. Triggered explicitly by phrases like "actually" or "scratch that", or implicitly by simply restating what you meant — Flow uses full-utterance context to strip false starts and filler words. Crucially it disambiguates intent: "I actually enjoyed the movie" does not trigger a correction because context indicates the word is content, not a command. This is an LLM-dependent behaviour, not a regex.

findings.topic: Flow Styles — tone modes assigned per app CATEGORY, not per app
findings.detail: Four presets: Formal, Casual, Very Casual (personal messages only), Excited (Work/Email/Other only). Flow auto-detects the active app and buckets it into one of four categories: Personal messages (Messages, WhatsApp, WeChat, Messenger), Work (Slack, Microsoft Teams), Email (Gmail, Outlook, Superhuman), Other (everything else). You assign a tone per category. Defaults: on iOS/Android Personal=Casual and Work/Email/Other=Formal; on Mac/Windows you pick during onboarding. Styles reshape tone AFTER transcription and apply only to new voice input. There is no fully custom style creation — personalisation instead comes from attaching 50–500 word writing samples (up to 5 per prompt) to custom polish prompts.

findings.topic: Transforms / Polish — voice-less AI editing of HIGHLIGHTED text via hotkey
findings.detail: This is the real 'edit existing text' surface (distinct from Command Mode). "Transforms let you rewrite text with AI — change tone, restructure, polish, or run your own custom prompts." Operates exclusively on selected text; with nothing selected it errors "Hey, select text first!". Default bindings: Polish = Opt+1 (Mac) / Win+Alt+1 (Windows); Prompt Engineer = Opt+2 / Win+Alt+2; View Diff = Opt+O / Win+Alt+O. A View Diff affordance exists — worth noting for w1 UX. Marketing framing: "highlight any text and rewrite it instantly with a custom AI rule — fix grammar, shift tone, translate, or reformat with a single keystroke." Limits: up to 8 custom transforms (one page says up to 9 custom prompts — minor doc inconsistency), 5 default toggleable rules, selections of 1–1,000 words, works "in most text fields where Flow can detect selected text" but fails in apps with custom editors. Mac + Windows only. Also triggerable from suggestion chips in Scratchpad, or automatically via auto-polish after dictation.

findings.topic: Command Mode — spoken instructions, Pro-gated (gating PLAUSIBLE not fully confirmed)
findings.detail: Separate hotkey from dictation: Mac Fn+Ctrl (or Cmd+Ctrl+Opt without Apple Fn), Windows Ctrl+Win+Alt. Hold, speak an instruction, release; ESC cancels. Up to 4 shortcuts of up to 3 keys, configured at Settings → Shortcuts → Command Mode. The docs page itself is thin: the only enumerated command is "press enter" — "Say 'press enter' at the end of a dictation and Flow inserts your text without the phrase, then presses Enter." It is described broadly as letting you "speak an instruction instead of typing it". CAVEAT / CONFLICT: search-surfaced snippets from the same docs domain state Command Mode "requires an active paid subscription or trial" and must be toggled on at Settings → Experimental (a section visible only to paying/trial users, alongside Press Enter Command and Bulk Import), and third-party reviews describe it as Pro-only voice-editing of highlighted text with commands like "make this more concise" or "translate to Polish". Direct fetches of the article did NOT surface those sentences. Treat Pro-gating as likely but not directly quoted; treat 'edits highlighted text' as UNVERIFIED for Command Mode specifically — that behaviour is definitively Transforms/Polish.

findings.topic: Context Awareness — the single most cloud-coupled feature; reads accessibility tree + optional screenshot
findings.detail: This is the deepest capability and the sharpest contrast with an on-device product. Verbatim from docs, context includes: "app info, textbox contents (before, selected, and after the cursor), on-screen text, variable and file names in coding apps, your user identifier within the app, the list of apps in your current session, a screenshot, and conversation history (participant IDs and message roles/content)." Two toggles at Settings → Data and Privacy: (a) Accessibility-text context — default ON on Mac and Windows; (b) Screen OCR — default OFF, captures a full-display screenshot to extract proper nouns. Interlock: screenshots only flow when BOTH toggles are on, and disabling accessibility-text context auto-disables Screen OCR. Transmission is explicit: context data is "sent to Wispr as part of each dictation request, unless Privacy Mode is on." Exclusion: "Password field contents are never read or included in context data" — but "custom or web-based password fields may be read like normal text fields" (standard macOS secure fields are auto-excluded). Enterprise admins can disable org-wide and lock the toggle. Windows quirk: context-aware formatting is skipped when dictating inside the Flow app window itself.

findings.topic: Dictionary — auto-learning from typed corrections, plus replacement rules, cloud-synced
findings.detail: Manual add on all four platforms via Dictionary → Add new. Auto-learning: an "auto-add to dictionary" setting notices when you correct a transcription by typing over it and adds the corrected spelling automatically; it "filters out common everyday words" so only distinctive/specialised terms are captured. Auto-learned entries carry a sparkle icon on desktop. Separate mechanism: "Correct a misspelling" replacement rules — you enter the wrong spelling Flow produces and it is auto-replaced during transcription. Tabs: All / Personal / Shared. Team dictionaries exist on Business/Team plans, and "personal dictionary words take precedence over team dictionary words" on conflict. Limits: 60 characters per word (59 on iOS), one replacement rule per word. Syncs across all devices automatically, effective immediately without restart.

findings.topic: Snippets — voice-triggered text expansion
findings.detail: Trigger phrase + expansion text. Spoken naturally mid-sentence; e.g. saying "send to my address" inserts the full address inline. "Trigger matching is case-insensitive, but expansions always use the exact casing you saved." Limits: trigger 60 chars, expansion 4,000 chars on desktop. Desktop supports rich text (bold, italic, lists, hyperlinks); iOS is plain text only. Search by trigger or expansion, sort newest/oldest/alphabetical, bulk import from JSON (desktop only), bulk delete/share. Team/Business plans get org-wide snippets with a shared badge; personal snippets take priority on trigger collision; personal snippets can be promoted to the team library. Syncs across devices with a manual refresh button and last-sync timestamp on desktop.

findings.topic: Multilingual — 100+ languages, but detection is per-SESSION not per-word
findings.detail: Supports "100+ languages, including regional variants such as British English, Canadian English, Swiss German, and Simplified or Traditional Chinese" (Wikipedia cites 104 languages; ~40% of usage English, 60% other). Manual selection or Auto-detect; guidance is that "fewer languages means more accurate detection" and recommends manually picking 2–3. KEY LIMITATION for parity scoping: language is detected at the START of each dictation session, not per word — "Switch languages mid-sentence and Flow transcribes the entire segment in one language." It handles occasional foreign words better than frequent alternation; Chinese-English mixing is explicitly problematic ("Flow may transcribe English words in Chinese characters or vice versa"). TRANSLITERATION: Hinglish (romanised Hindi mixed with English) is a first-class listed language and must be selected explicitly — choosing Hindi alone will not produce it. Non-English accuracy lags English; French gets automatic typographic spacing before certain punctuation. No real-time translation-while-dictating is documented (translation appears only as a Transforms rewrite rule).

findings.topic: History storage — LOCAL by default on desktop, with a separate cloud-sync toggle
findings.detail: Important nuance and a genuine on-device precedent: "Transcripts are stored locally on each device. Deleting history on one device does not affect your other devices." Local data storage is configured at Settings → Data and Privacy with three options: store data, auto-delete every 24 hours, or never store locally. This is "separate from Cloud Sync, which controls whether transcription data is stored on Wispr's servers." Audio is deleted after 14 days. Deleting locally does not delete server-side copies — Cloud Sync must be disabled separately. History appears on the Home screen grouped by date (Today, Yesterday, then by date). Per-item actions documented on mobile: tap to copy, tap a failed one to retry, swipe for Flag/Retry/Copy, long-press for Copy/Retry/Report/Delete. SEARCH over desktop dictation history is NOT documented — mark unverified; iOS Notes are described as searchable across devices.

findings.topic: Scratchpad / Notes — cloud-synced voice notes with AI suggestion chips
findings.detail: Listed in the desktop sidebar as "Scratchpad (Beta): Cloud-synced voice notes with Recents tab". Transforms can be triggered from context-aware "suggestion chips" generated based on note content. Notes can be pinned in both the Notes hub and the Scratchpad sidebar. On iOS it is a dedicated tab ("Scratchpad (Notes): Voice notes grouped by date") and iOS Notes support dictating and searching notes across devices, plus lock screen widgets and Siri shortcuts. NOTE: the dedicated Scratchpad help article body could not be retrieved (page returned navigation chrome only), so depth beyond the above is unverified.

findings.topic: Notetaker — system-audio meeting capture with NO bot joining (Mac only, beta)
findings.detail: "No bot joins your calls. Notetaker captures audio directly from your system without adding a participant to the meeting." Detects Google Meet (via Chrome/Edge/Brave), Zoom, and Microsoft Teams; calendar-aware so it knows which meeting you're in and offers recording contextually. Captures both system audio ("Capture what others say" permission) and mic input; if the mic drops it continues on system audio only. Requires three things: System Audio permission, Microphone access, and Private Cloud Sync enabled — "Wispr Notetaker requires this." Mac only: "Available on: Mac. If you don't see Notetaker in your app yet, it hasn't rolled out to your account." Free plan includes it with a weekly cap on meeting notes; paid plans get higher limits and extended retention. Local audio retained 90 days by default (allows meeting resumption); transcripts and summaries stored in the cloud. Persistent consent notice during recording: "Always get consent when transcribing others." Surrounding feature set: live transcript, meeting notes editor, Flow Summaries, Notetaker hub, Ask Wispr (chat with your meetings and notes), Pre-reads (pre-meeting briefings), sharing, and dictating during a meeting.

findings.topic: Insights / analytics surface — exact composition of the screen the user screenshotted
findings.detail: Lives in the left sidebar of the desktop app (Mac and Windows ONLY — no iOS/Android). Three tabs: Your Usage → Your Voice → Leaderboard (not all shown to every user). YOUR USAGE contains: (1) WPM — an animated semicircular/radial gauge showing average dictation speed as a rounded whole number plus percentile, labelled "Compared to global typing speeds", percentile ranging "Top 0.1%" to "Top 99%", with a note that most users see a high percentile because dictation beats typing; (2) "Corrections by Flow" — the 'fixes made' tile, counting automatic transcription fixes including "filler words like 'um' and 'like'" plus dictionary and snippet substitutions, split into two rows (words corrected / dictionary fixes); (3) Total Words Dictated — cumulative running count with a month-over-month badge (e.g. "+12% this month"), hover reveals "{current} words compared to {previous} words this time last month"; (4) Desktop App Usage Breakdown — a HORIZONTAL BAR CHART by app CATEGORY (personal messages, work messages, emails, AI prompts, documents, other), each row showing word count and percentage, colour-coded by rank (top darkest, 2nd/3rd medium, rest lightest), with hover intensity labels "Light usage" (<1,000 words), "Moderate usage" (1,000–9,999), "Power usage" (10,000+); (5) Usage Streak Heatmap — calendar view, current-streak days highlighted with a glow that appears only when the streak exceeds 1 day, other active days shaded by word count, extending back to account creation or 2025-03-01 "whichever is more recent", with arrows jumping back 4 weeks per click. Note: the desktop breakdown excludes mobile dictation, and the Your Voice tab requires the "Store Normally" data policy. A smaller stats card also appears on Home showing streak, average WPM, and total words, with large counts abbreviated (e.g. "1.22M words").

findings.topic: Insights — Leaderboard tab and social sharing carousel
findings.detail: LEADERBOARD is visible only to Pro Team members, Enterprise users, or users with 2+ same-domain colleagues; non-eligible users see locked previews prompting "Create team", "Request to join", or "Upgrade to enterprise". Features podium + paginated table views (20 rows/page), sort by Total words / WPM / Current daily streak / Desktop words / Mobile words, time ranges "This week" or "All time" (WPM and streak only for All time), hourly refresh, and a "Jump to Me" control. Enterprise admins get a "See team usage" button into an Admin Portal dashboard and can toggle "Hide team leaderboard" org-wide. SHARE opens a carousel of up to 12 branded cards: Flow Highlights, Total Words Dictated, Flow Streak, How Fast You Flow (WPM), Your Flow Activity (heatmap), Where You Flow (desktop breakdown), Your Voice Profile, Flow Superlatives, When You Flow the Most. Cards can be copied, downloaded as an image, or shared to X/LinkedIn — social sharing "copies the card image to your clipboard and opens the platform's compose page" pre-filled with "Check out my Wispr Flow Insights!". There is also a documented flow to add Wispr Flow to your LinkedIn profile. This is a deliberate growth-loop surface, not just analytics.

findings.topic: App structure — menu bar vs main window vs floating Flow Bar (three surfaces)
findings.detail: MAIN WINDOW ("Hub") with left sidebar: Home (history by date, total word count, dictation shortcut, stats card with streak/avg WPM/total words), Notifications (bell, remote notifications), Dictionary (All/Personal/Shared tabs), Snippets, Style (tone by location: Personal message / Work messages / Email / Other), Scratchpad (Beta), Insights, and Settings & Help plus Refer/Invite depending on plan. FLOATING FLOW BAR: a bottom-of-screen floating bubble with a mic button, language picker, and a right-click menu (Hide / Settings / Microphone / History / Paste); it can be moved and docked, and snoozed. MENU BAR (Mac) / system tray (Windows): app shortcuts, meeting countdown display, and options. Mobile differs: iOS uses a 5-tab bar plus a Flow Keyboard with a top bar (settings, Undo/Redo, Voice Edit, Add to Dictionary, mic button, style pill); Android uses a 4-tab bar plus a floating Flow Bubble with configurable size/opacity.

findings.topic: Settings surface areas — full enumeration
findings.detail: Desktop settings sections: General, System, Notetaker, Connectors, MCP, Vibe Coding, Experimental — plus Account, Plans & Billing, and Data & Privacy. General holds Shortcuts, Microphone, and Languages. System holds Launch at login, Show Flow Bar, sound toggles, Auto-add to dictionary, and other features. Data and Privacy holds Context awareness, Screen OCR, local data storage policy (store / auto-delete every 24h / never store locally), and Cloud Sync. Experimental holds Command Mode, Press Enter Command, and Bulk Import and is understood to be paid-plans-only. Vibe Coding holds native Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code integration, File Tagging, and Variable Recognition setup. Accessibility settings support keyboard-only operation, screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, TalkBack), and honouring the system reduced-motion setting. Notification preferences are customisable by category. The app interface language is itself changeable.

findings.topic: Onboarding flow on macOS — step by step
findings.detail: (1) Launch → "Sign in via browser" opens the default browser → authenticate with Google, Apple, Microsoft, SSO, or email/password → session transfers back to the desktop app. (2) Permissions screen with three sequential cards, each auto-advancing when granted, and "Flow re-checks permissions before letting you continue": Microphone; Accessibility (so Flow can "insert spoken words into other apps"); System Audio (Notetaker only, required on newer macOS). (3) Intro screens. (4) Attribution question "Tell us about yourself" with predefined options and an "Other" free-text field. (5) Privacy notice review. (6) Microphone test with audio visualisation. (7) Shortcut configuration — press your desired combo or accept the default (Fn, or Ctrl+Opt). (8) Language selection — specific languages or auto-detect. (9) Practice demos with on-screen prompts. (10) Privacy preferences. (11) Land on the Flow Hub with a welcome message, stats, and the dictation shortcut highlighted in the welcome header for new users. There is also a product-aware onboarding branch letting macOS users choose dictation, Notetaker, or both, plus team-aware onboarding and guided product tours.

findings.topic: Pricing and account model
findings.detail: FREE: $0. 2,000 words/week on desktop, 1,000/week on iPhone, unlimited on Android. Includes speech-to-text, Notetaker (Mac only, weekly meeting cap), speaker identification, meeting questions, MCP access, calendar/Slack integration. PRO: $15/user/month monthly, or $12/user/month annual (20% discount). Unlimited dictation, advanced AI thinking models, early feature access, prioritised support, centralised billing, shared dictionary/snippets, extended meeting retention, basic usage dashboards. ENTERPRISE: custom pricing. Adds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 compliance, HIPAA BAA, admin controls, audit logs, MDM, domain management, SAML SSO/SCIM, dedicated support, volume discounts, advanced analytics, enforced model-training opt-out. Account is mandatory — there is no anonymous/local-only mode; sign-in is required at first launch. Wikipedia reports ~19% paid conversion, >50% monthly user growth, ~80% six-month retention, and $81M total raised (Series A led by Menlo Ventures, extension led by Notable Capital).

findings.topic: CLOUD DEPENDENCY — the decisive finding for w1's positioning
findings.detail: Wispr's own documentation is unambiguous. Data Controls page: "Transcription always occurs on the cloud. This is the best way for us to provide accurate, low latency transcription." Security FAQ: "Wispr Flow runs entirely in the cloud and is delivered as multi-tenant SaaS, hosted with a major US cloud provider" and "Wispr's backend must decrypt audio to perform transcription." The What-is-Flow doc states Flow requires an active internet connection and does not support offline operation. Models are "a combination of open-source models and proprietary LLM providers" (Baseten confirms fine-tuned Llama on AWS). Even the strongest privacy configuration is cloud-processing-with-no-retention, not local processing: with Privacy Mode ON and Private Cloud Sync OFF you get "zero data retention for all audio and transcript data" — "Audio and transcripts are processed in real time and discarded after the request completes" — but the audio still leaves the device. Privacy Mode means "none of your dictation data (i.e. audio, transcript, edits) will be used to evaluate, train, or improve AI models, by Wispr or any third party", and is permanently locked on for HIPAA BAA signatories. Wispr holds zero-data-retention agreements with all third-party AI providers. Certifications: SOC 2 Type I completed April 2026 (A-LIGN), ISO 27001:2022 Stage 1 completed April 2026 with Stage 2 in progress, HIPAA BAA available, annual third-party pen testing (note: the marketing site claims SOC 2 Type II while the security FAQ says Type I — inconsistency worth flagging).

findings.topic: Which features are cloud-dependent vs on-device — parity scoping table
findings.detail: HARD CLOUD (cannot exist without a server round-trip in Wispr's design): ASR transcription itself; Smart Formatting; Backtrack filler/false-start removal; Flow Styles tone rewriting; Transforms/Polish and all custom prompts; Command Mode; Context Awareness payload (accessibility tree + screenshot + conversation history are UPLOADED per request); auto-detect language selection; Notetaker transcription, Flow Summaries, Ask Wispr and Pre-reads; the MCP server (remote, URL-based); cross-device sync of dictionary, snippets, styles and Scratchpad; Insights percentile ranking (requires global comparison data); Leaderboard; team/shared dictionary and snippets; admin portal and usage dashboards. ON-DEVICE / LOCAL TODAY: dictation history transcript storage (local by default, three-way policy); Notetaker's raw audio capture and 90-day local audio cache; clipboard-based text insertion and accessibility-tree reading (the READ is local — the transmission is what's cloud); hotkey handling and Flow Bar UI. NEUTRAL / LOCALLY COMPUTABLE: total words, WPM, streaks, corrections count, per-app-category breakdown, heatmap — all derivable from local history, EXCEPT the percentile and leaderboard. Implication: w1 can plausibly reach parity on the dictation loop, dictionary, snippets, history, insights (minus percentile), and local formatting; the gap concentrates on LLM-quality rewriting, screenshot/OCR context, and meeting summarisation.

findings.topic: Session limits — a real constraint worth matching or beating
findings.detail: Desktop (Mac and Windows) dictation sessions warn at 19 minutes and stop automatically at a 20-minute maximum; this was itself shipped as an improvement ("Longer dictation sessions — now up to 20 minutes"). Android caps at ~5 minutes with a warning at 4 minutes. Wikipedia describes these as configurable "Flow Sessions" with microphone access timeouts. An on-device product has no per-request cost pressure and could plausibly remove this cap entirely as a differentiator.

findings.topic: Developer/IDE features — Variable Recognition, File Tagging, Vibe Coding settings
findings.detail: Settings → Vibe coding enables native integration with Cursor, Windsurf, and VS Code. File Tagging automatically tags files in the IDE when you name them by voice — saying "fix the auth issue in userService.ts" references the file directly; it works in Cursor and Windsurf only. Variable Recognition improves handling of code vocabulary and syntax, parsing camelCase, snake_case and acronyms, preserving spacing, and understanding CLI/dev jargon; it has a guided setup flow. The personal dictionary is also positioned as learning variable names and function names. Shipped around March 2026. Separate docs cover using Flow with Linux, WSL and terminal applications, and with remote desktops (RDP/Citrix/VDI).

findings.topic: Routing and integrations beyond plain insertion
findings.detail: Flow can "route dictation directly to Slack, Email, or Calendar with keyboard shortcuts" — i.e. dedicated hotkeys that send dictated text to a destination app rather than the focused field. There is a Connectors settings section and calendar/Slack integration is listed even on the Free plan. The MCP server is remote (paste a URL), read-only, exposes Notetaker meeting notes/summaries/briefs but explicitly NOT dictation history or voice recordings, works with Claude (web/desktop/Cowork), ChatGPT (web, Developer mode), Cursor, and VS Code with Copilot, and requires Notetaker plus Cloud Sync, Mac only.

findings.topic: Platform support and system requirements
findings.detail: macOS 12.0+ on Apple Silicon and Intel; Windows 10/11 64-bit; iOS 18.3+; Android (Beta). Insights, Transforms/Polish, Command Mode, and Context Awareness are desktop-only. Notetaker is Mac-only. Known criticisms from reviews include high system resource usage, startup delays, occasional punctuation/grammar issues in certain apps, and latency creep as the user base grew (~40% MoM as of March 2026). Wikipedia also notes Wispr confirmed the app "can read the device user's keystrokes", which raised security concerns — relevant context for w1's privacy positioning.

open_questions: Command Mode gating is not directly confirmed: the help article itself contains no plan-requirement or Settings → Experimental sentence, yet search snippets attributed to the same docs domain and third-party reviews both state it is paid-only and toggled in Settings → Experimental. Recommend confirming in-app or via a Pro account before treating Pro-gating as fact.

Whether Command Mode operates on selected/highlighted text is UNVERIFIED. The docs only ever demonstrate 'press enter'. Third-party reviews describe 'make this more concise' / 'translate to Polish' on highlighted text, but that behaviour is definitively documented for Transforms/Polish, not Command Mode — the two may have been conflated by reviewers.

Search over desktop dictation history is not documented anywhere. History is grouped by date with per-item copy/retry/delete actions, and Snippets and Dictionary both have search, but no transcript search is described for the desktop Home screen. iOS Notes are described as searchable. Needs in-app confirmation.

The Scratchpad help article body could not be retrieved (returned navigation chrome only), so its depth — voice editing of notes, search, export, retention — is only partially known from the app-navigation article.
The Auto Cleanup (Beta) article is explicitly unpublished ('This article is not currently available'), so that feature is entirely unverified despite being listed in the Using Wispr Flow collection.
Transform count is inconsistent across docs: one page says 'up to 8 custom transforms', another says 'up to 9 custom prompts'. Minor, but worth noting if replicating limits.

Compliance claim conflict: the marketing site and pricing page claim SOC 2 Type II, while the security FAQ states SOC 2 Type I completed April 2026 with ISO 27001 Stage 2 still in progress. The FAQ is the more conservative and likely more accurate source.

The official changelog URL (wisprflow.ai/changelog) returned 404, so release history was reconstructed from a third-party aggregator (releasebot.io) rather than first-party. Version-level feature dating should be treated as approximate.

No first-party statement was found on whether any part of the ASR runs on-device as a fallback (e.g. wake-word or VAD). All evidence points to fully server-side transcription, but the absence of a local VAD claim is inferred rather than stated.
Notetaker's exact free-plan weekly meeting cap number is not published in the docs reviewed — only that a cap exists and paid plans are higher.

summary: Complete design-system extraction of the BAPS Tracker Next.js app (Next 15.3.9 / React 19 / Tailwind v4.1.4 CSS-first, NO tailwind.config file). The system is a shadcn "base-nova"/neutral variant re-skinned onto a ported "Content Studio" demo palette: 19 HSL-triplet semantic tokens in :root + .dark (class-based dark mode, cookie-driven SSR, warm-grey hue-50 dark theme rather than shadcn blue-grey), 7 legacy hex --tracker-* constants, a 0.5rem-base radius scale with a deliberate rounded-xl passthrough, Onest (sans) + JetBrains Mono (mono, user-togglable app-wide with a shifted weight scale), 13 shadcn primitives, Tailwind's stock shadow scale, lucide-react icons at 14/16/18/20/22px, and a three-column flex shell (240/56px glass sidebar - rounded-3xl opaque content panel - 340px-default resizable glass right rail) floating on a fixed 18px CSS dot-grid lattice with a cursor spotlight. Per-enum colours (priority/avatar/pastel/stage) deliberately live in TypeScript, not CSS tokens.

findings.topic: Build setup — Tailwind v4 CSS-first, no config file
findings.detail: There is NO tailwind.config.js/ts anywhere. Tailwind v4.1.4 is wired purely through PostCSS (plugins: ["@tailwindcss/postcss"]) and globals.css does the whole configuration via `@import "tailwindcss"; @import "tw-animate-css";` plus an `@theme inline {}` block. components.json confirms it with "tailwind": { "config": "" } (empty string). Exactly ONE stylesheet exists in the repo: src/app/globals.css, 372 lines. Deps: tailwindcss 4.1.4, @tailwindcss/postcss 4.1.4, tw-animate-css 1.4.0, class-variance-authority 0.7.1, clsx 2.1.1, tailwind-merge 3.5.0. cn() = twMerge(clsx(inputs)).

findings.topic: Radius scale — exact computed values

findings.topic: Fonts — exact families, loader, variables
findings.detail: next/font/google only; no @font-face and no local font files anywhere in the repo. `Onest({ variable: "--font-onest", subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap", fallback: ["system-ui", "-apple-system", "sans-serif"] })` and `JetBrains_Mono({ variable: "--font-jetbrains-mono", subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap", fallback: ["ui-monospace", "SFMono-Regular", "Menlo", "monospace"] })`. NO weight array is passed to either — both load as variable fonts across the full axis. Both variables are applied on <body> alongside `antialiased`. Budget note in source: latin subset plus variable axis keeps it to at most 2 font files under 60 kB.

findings.topic: Dark mode mechanism — class, not media query
findings.detail: CLASS-based via `@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *))` — note the descendant form. Resolution order: (1) the server reads the mt-dark cookie in the root layout and stamps the <html> class before paint via htmlClassFromPrefs(); (2) a synchronous inline BOOT_SCRIPT, the first node in <body>, handles FIRST VISIT ONLY — if the cookie is absent and matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)') matches, it adds .dark (it also clears the retired localStorage key mt-mono); (3) PrefsProvider reconciles React state to the DOM post-hydration. prefers-color-scheme is therefore a first-visit default, never the ongoing mechanism. Cookies: mt-dark ('1'/'0' -> .dark), mt-mono-v2 ('1'/'0' -> .mono), mt-tips ('0' -> .tips-off; default ON, absent != '0'). Cookie max-age 31536000 (1 year), path=/, samesite=lax. <html> also carries suppressHydrationWarning.

findings.topic: Mono-font mode — a whole second typographic system
findings.detail: `html.mono body` swaps the app to `var(--font-jetbrains-mono), ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace` with `letter-spacing: -0.045em` and `font-weight: 300`, and shifts the entire weight scale down one step: `html.mono .font-normal { 300 }`, `html.mono .font-medium { 400 }`, `html.mono .font-semibold { 500 }`. Toggled from the topbar via a Type/Code icon pair. Any rebuild must carry the tracking and weight shift or the mono mode reads as heavy and wide.

findings.topic: Base layer — global resets and browser chrome
findings.detail: `* { @apply border-border }` sets the global default border colour. `html, body, #root { height: 100% }`. `body { @apply bg-background text-foreground font-sans antialiased }`. Custom scrollbars: `::-webkit-scrollbar { width: 10px; height: 10px }`; thumb `@apply rounded-full bg-muted-foreground/25` with `border: 3px solid transparent; background-clip: content-box`; track transparent. One utility: `.pb-safe { padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom) }`. Mobile scale-up: `@media (max-width: 767px) { body { zoom: 1.07 } }` — load-bearing, since several component comments compute phone pixel budgets against the resulting ~336 CSS px at a 360px device width.

findings.topic: Shell anatomy — root container and exact gutters
findings.detail: AppShell root: `<div className="relative flex h-full overflow-hidden bg-background md:gap-3 md:p-3">` — a 3-column flex row with a 12px gutter and 12px page padding at md+, zero on mobile. findings.topic: Glass materials — the four custom surface recipes
findings.detail: .card-glass: background rgb(255 255 255 / 0.55); backdrop-filter blur(14px) saturate(1.5) plus -webkit- prefix; dark background rgb(30 30 27 / 0.5). Under @media (hover: hover) it also gets `transition: border-color 0.2s ease` and `:hover { border-color: hsl(var(--foreground) / 0.18) }` — hover is colour-only, nothing moves. .liquid-glass: background rgb(255 255 255 / 0.3); blur(36px) saturate(2); border-color rgb(0 0 0 / 0.09); box-shadow inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.5); dark background rgb(32 32 29 / 0.35), border-color rgb(255 255 255 / 0.13), box-shadow inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.07). .liquid-glass-pill: background rgb(255 255 255 / 0.55); blur(8px); border 1px solid rgb(0 0 0 / 0.07); dark background rgb(255 255 255 / 0.09), border-color rgb(255 255 255 / 0.12). These rules are UNLAYERED, so they beat Tailwind utilities — exploited deliberately to override Card's opaque bg-card in AuthCard.

findings.topic: Dot-grid backdrop — exact lattice values
findings.detail: .dot-grid sets `--mx: -999px; --my: -999px` and paints `radial-gradient(rgb(156 163 175 / 0.18) 0.8px, transparent 1.1px)` at `background-size: 18px 18px` with `background-attachment: fixed`, which anchors one continuous lattice across every frosted surface. .dot-grid::after is an absolute inset-0 pointer-events-none layer of brighter dots `radial-gradient(rgb(156 163 175 / 0.55) 1.6px, transparent 2px)` revealed through `mask-image: radial-gradient(120px circle at var(--mx) var(--my), black 15%, transparent 95%)` (with -webkit-mask-image). .dot-grid-paint is the same base lattice for painting crisp dots ON TOP of frosted surfaces (blur erases the ones behind). Dark mode lowers alphas to 0.08 (base and paint) and 0.3 (::after). The <DotGrid> component only writes --mx/--my imperatively from a passive pointermove listener (no React state, no rAF, no canvas), parks them at -999px on pointerleave, and skips the listener entirely under prefers-reduced-motion.

findings.topic: Tinted tag materials — the data-driven colour system
findings.detail: .tint-tag { background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--tag) 12%, transparent); color: var(--tag) }; dark: { background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--tag) 26%, transparent); color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--tag) 52%, white) }. .pastel-tag { background: var(--pastel-bg); color: var(--pastel-fg) }; dark: { background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--pastel-fg) 24%, transparent); color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--pastel-fg) 58%, white) }. Consumers pass a single hex as a CSS custom property and the rule does the light/dark maths — this is how one hex per stage, priority or skill renders correctly in both themes. TintBadge classes: `tint-tag inline-flex items-center whitespace-nowrap rounded-full px-2.5 py-0.5 text-xs font-medium`. PastelPill classes: `pastel-tag inline-flex items-center whitespace-nowrap rounded-full px-2 py-0.5 text-[10.5px] font-medium`.

findings.topic: Tooltip system — a body-level singleton, not Radix
findings.detail: There is NO Radix tooltip primitive. One `.app-tip` div is appended to <body> by <TooltipLayer/> and positioned by JS via pointerover/pointermove event delegation on any [data-tip] element. CSS: `position: fixed; z-index: 2147483647; pointer-events: none; white-space: nowrap; border-radius: 6px; background: hsl(var(--foreground)); color: hsl(var(--background)); padding: 3px 8px; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 500; line-height: 1.4; opacity: 0; transition: opacity 0.1s ease`. `.app-tip.show { opacity: 1; animation: tip-pop 0.18s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.9, 0.3, 1.4) }`, where @keyframes tip-pop is `from { transform: translateX(-6px) scale(0.94); opacity: 0 }`. Placement: centred over the target, 12px above; flips to 16px below when it would clip the top; clamped 4px inside the horizontal edges. Suppressed entirely when .tips-off is on <html>. Text is set via textContent only (explicit OWASP A03 note). Listeners are pointer* (not mouse*) so pen and touch work.

findings.topic: Shadow scale — Tailwind stock, no custom tokens
findings.detail: No --shadow-* is defined in @theme; the app uses Tailwind's default scale sparingly. Total usage across src/**/*.tsx: shadow-none 9, shadow-sm 5, shadow-lg 3, shadow-xl 2, shadow-2xl 2, shadow-black/5 1. Assignments: `md:shadow-sm` on the main content panel; `shadow-sm` on Input, SelectTrigger and the Switch thumb; `shadow-lg` on SelectContent and the mobile nav bar; `shadow-xl` on the workspace-switcher popover; `shadow-2xl` on DialogContent and SheetContent; `shadow-xl shadow-black/5` on AuthCard. The only hand-written box-shadows in CSS are the two `inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.5)` and `/ 0.07` highlights on .liquid-glass.

findings.topic: Animation vocabulary — keyframes and utilities
findings.detail: Custom keyframes: fade-up (opacity 0 + translateY(8px) to none), grow-y (from scaleY(0)), grow-x (from scaleX(0)), draw-stroke (stroke-dashoffset 1 to 0), dash-flow (to stroke-dashoffset -20), tip-pop. Utilities: `.animate-fade-up { animation: fade-up 0.3s ease both }`; `.animate-grow-y { transform-origin: bottom; animation: grow-y 0.6s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.7, 0.2, 1) both }`; `.animate-grow-x { transform-origin: left; animation: grow-x 0.7s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.7, 0.2, 1) both }`; `.animate-draw { stroke-dasharray: 1; animation: draw-stroke 1.1s ease-out both }`; `.animate-dash-flow { animation: dash-flow 1.2s linear infinite }`. Radix enter/exit utilities (data-[state=open]:animate-in, fade-in-0, zoom-in-95, slide-in-from-*) come from tw-animate-css. A global @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block neutralises every animation and transition on *, *::before, *::after to 0.001ms with animation-iteration-count 1 and scroll-behavior auto, all !important. The old six-dot logo spin/shimmer keyframes were deleted in the 2026-07-30 rebrand.

findings.topic: Typography conventions — an arbitrary-px-heavy scale
findings.detail: The app leans on arbitrary px sizes far more than the Tailwind scale. Tally across src/**/*.tsx — arbitrary: text-[13px] 130 (the dominant UI size: nav rows, buttons, crumbs, search, rail controls, console tabs), text-[11px] 100 (section labels, sublines), text-[12px] 57, text-[10px] 34, text-[15px] 32 (tile/empty-state/card titles and the sidebar wordmark), text-[10.5px] 30 (pastel pills, count badges, mobile nav labels), text-[9px] 10, text-[9.5px] 6, text-[8px] 4, text-[7px] 5, text-[11.5px] 3, text-[17px] 1 (auth wordmark), text-[6px] 1. Tailwind scale: text-sm 122, text-xs 75, text-lg 16, text-xl 14, text-base 6, text-2xl 3, text-3xl 1 (the KPI value: `text-3xl font-medium tracking-tight`). findings.topic: Brand mark — exact SVG geometry
findings.detail: The logo is pure inline SVG; the component references no image asset. viewBox='0 0 100 100', four copies of a single 50x50 tile path `M25 0H46Q50 0 50 4V25L25 50H4Q0 50 0 46V25Z` translated to (0,0), (50,0), (0,50), (50,50). Each tile is a square chamfered at its top-left and bottom-right corners at exactly half the side and rounded (r=4) at the other two; the facing chamfers of neighbouring tiles cut the diagonal channels through the mark. Default class: `h-[30px] w-[30px] shrink-0 fill-foreground` — it fills currentColor so it inverts in dark mode with no second asset, and it is presentational with no hooks (safe in a server tree). The same path is deliberately duplicated in src/components/auth/auth-shell.tsx (AuthLogo, default h-7 w-7), public/favicon.svg and public/offline.html so each surface stays standalone.

findings.topic: PWA and browser theme colours
findings.detail: viewport export: viewportFit 'cover'; themeColor = [{ media: '(prefers-color-scheme: light)', color: '#ffffff' }, { media: '(prefers-color-scheme: dark)', color: '#1b1b19' }] — #1b1b19 is the hex rendering of the dark --background (50 3% 10%). manifest.webmanifest: name and short_name 'BAPS Tracker', display 'standalone', start_url '/', background_color '#ffffff', theme_color '#ffffff', icons 192 any / 512 any / 512 maskable. metadata: title and applicationName 'BAPS Tracker', description 'Multi-project content tracker for the BAPS UK content team', icons favicon.svg (listed first, inverts with prefers-color-scheme) then favicon-32.png, apple-touch-icon.png at 180x180, appleWebApp { capable: true, statusBarStyle: 'default', title: 'BAPS Tracker' }.

findings.topic: Breakpoint usage — the shell's three responsive tiers
findings.detail: Stock Tailwind breakpoints, used at three decision points. sm (640px): the topbar pref-toggle group, sign-out, profile avatar and the labelled person-filter appear; view-pill labels appear; the Sheet 'adaptive' side switches from a bottom sheet to a right drawer; EmptyState padding goes p-8 to sm:p-12. md (768px): the sidebar appears (hidden md:flex), the shell gutter md:gap-3 md:p-3 turns on, the mobile nav disappears, the topbar crumb and desktop search appear, main padding goes pb-28 to md:pb-4, and body zoom:1.07 turns off. lg (1024px): the right rail appears (hidden lg:flex) and becomes the host of task detail instead of the adaptive Sheet — duplicated as RAIL_HOST_QUERY = '(min-width: 1024px)' in a useSyncExternalStore-based useMediaQuery whose SSR/pre-mount snapshot is hard-coded false so the rail/Sheet pair never double-renders.

open_questions: Two parallel colour registries exist for the same concepts — the v1 palette (avatar-color.ts / project-color.ts / priority.ts, e.g. HIGH = #2563eb) and the demo-parity palette (demo-parity.ts, e.g. HIGH = #D98E5F). The v1 set is described in-source as grandfathered for un-migrated pages. A rebuild should pick one per axis; the demo-parity set appears to be the intended one.

The --tracker-* hex tokens have no .dark override, so bg-tracker-surface-sunken (#f2f4f7) renders near-white on the Dialog/Sheet close buttons in dark mode, and Checkbox/Switch checked states use #2563eb rather than the theme --primary (217.2 70% 62% in dark). Source comments call these scheduled for retirement — replicate the quirk or fix it in the rebuild?

PRIORITY_HEX.CRITICAL is an explicitly flagged placeholder reusing HIGH's #D98E5F, and PriorityPill labels CRITICAL as 'High'. Still unresolved in-source (awaiting a design call). #991B1B is reserved for blocked and must not be used for it.

No shadow tokens are defined in @theme, so shadow-sm/lg/xl/2xl are whatever Tailwind 4.1.4 ships. If the rebuild pins a different Tailwind minor the shadow rendering can drift silently — worth pinning exactly or promoting shadows to explicit tokens.
globals.css styles `#root { height: 100% }`, but a Next App Router tree has no #root element — a dead rule carried over from the Vite demo this was ported from.

The unread-badge hue #D98E5F is duplicated as an inline style literal in three components rather than living in demo-parity.ts alongside the other enum hexes; worth promoting to a named constant in the rebuild.
